newsitem.title: FRANCE: OLYMPICS-LILLE FAILS TO CONVINCE FRENCH MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-LILLE FAILS TO CONVINCE FRENCH MINISTER.

text.p: Lille, capital of Flanders in the heart of the old northern France mining region, hopes to convince the world it is the ideal location for the 2004 Olympic Games.
As yet is has failed to convince even the French Sports Minister Guy Drut.
Last month the former Olympic high hurdles champion gave the official government reaction to Lille's bid.

"Obviously Lille has weaknesses, especially in terms of equipment compared to others," Drut commented. "It is obvious that Rome, Athens or Buenos Aires have better sports and touristic facilities, which already exist."
The International Olympic Committee have already pointed out that the sports venues would be too widespread while only 2,640 hotel beds are currently available in the town itself.

Local officials maintain that Lille is ideally situated close to Brussels, Paris and London with more than 100 million people able to reach the city within two hours, including visitors from south-east England via the Channel tunnel.

The Lille bid was launched by 200 local businessmen and prominent personalities with an estimated budget of 7.2 billion francs ($1.4 billion) to come out of broadcasting rights, ticket sales and sponsors.
Lille would have to invest 3.7 billion francs ($700 million), including three billion for the sports facilities. The French state and local councils would each contribute half the amount.
At least Lille, ruled by former Prime Minister Pierre Mauroy, has won one important battle when the the French Olympic Committee decided to support its bid ahead of Lyon.
The victory was seen as revenge for the industrial north and, especially the Rhone-Alps region, which hosted Winter Olympics in 1968 and again in 1992.
Organisers, who have adopted the slogan "Our bid is a human size bid", believe a successful bid would create 200,000 jobs in a region hard hit by unemployment.
The main sites would be spread along a 20-km "L'Arc Olympique" containing 70 percent of the sports facilities, the Olympic villages and the media centres.

Lille, the birthplace of General Charles de Gaulle, has a strong sports tradition. The region boasts two first division soccer teams in Lille and Lens and regularly hosts a grand prix athletics meeting and rugby union internationals.
"The other bidding towns have a past, we have a future," says Mauroy.
